0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
See how you translated the term **Gittith** in the superscription to Psalm 8.

1.q: הַ֭רְנִינוּ לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים עוּזֵּ֑⁠נוּ הָ֝רִ֗יעוּ לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֥י יַעֲקֹֽב
1.note: These two phrases **Shout joyfully to God, our strength** and **shout out to the God of Jacob** mean basically the same thing. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on translating parallel phrases, see the Introduction to this psalm. Alternate translation: [Shout with great joy to God who is the strength of Jacob’s descendants]

Asaph is saying what he wants the people of Israel to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech and follow the decision of your team, here and throughout this psalm, of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that all shout joyfully to God, our strength; you should all shout out]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who strengthens us]

3.note: Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [also blow a shofar at the full moon]

4.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because it is a statute for Israel]

4.q: חֹ֣ק לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל ה֑וּא מִ֝שְׁפָּ֗ט לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֥י יַעֲקֹֽב
4.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **statute** and **judgment**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [it is something that God decreed, what the God of Jacob decided]

5.note: The pronoun **He** refers to God, and the pronoun **he** in **when he went out** refers to Joseph (representing Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God set it as a testimony in Joseph when Israel went out]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **testimony**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as something to be observed]

The name **Joseph** represents the people of Israel, particularly the tribes descended from Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [among the people of Israel]
Here, **lip** represents language or speech. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a tongue]

6.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. His speech continues through verse 16. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a first-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a first-level quotation.

The phrase **I removed his shoulder from the burden** represents Yahweh completely liberating Israel from slavery in Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I freed him from his slavery]

The pronouns **his** refer to the people of Israel collectively. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the shoulder of my people from the burden; their palms passed from the basket]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When you were suffering]

Yahweh is speaking as if he were concealed within **the secret place of thunder**. This represents God’s awesome and hidden presence in the storm. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the thunderstorm where I was hidden]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to describe a hidden place that is associated with thunder. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the place hidden by thunder]
The word **Meribah** is the name of a desert place.

8.note: Here, **if you would listen to me** introduces the first part of a possible condition. Yahweh will only do the things described in verses 13–16 if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen.

Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, a deep longing for Israel to obey. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Yahweh was feeling. Alternate translation: [Israel, I so deeply wish you would listen to me]

9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **foreignness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to a foreign god]

10.note: Yahweh is speaking as if Israel’s dependence on him were opening a mouth wide to be fed. This represents trusting God to provide abundantly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Depend on me completely, and I will provide for you abundantly]

The word translated as **Open wide** is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [If you open wide your mouth, then I will fill it]

11.note: Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the commands he gave in verses 8–10 and the response of the people. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, my people did not listen]

Here, **voice** represents Yahweh’s commands and instructions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to my commands]

12.note: The term translated as **So** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Therefore I sent them away]

Here, **heart** represents the will and inner attitude of the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the stubbornness of their wills]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **stubbornness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with their stubborn hearts]

Yahweh is speaking of how the people lived as if that were a path that they were walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they lived according to their own plans]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsels**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way they themselves chose]

13.q: ל֗וּ עַ֭מִּ⁠י שֹׁמֵ֣עַֽ לִ֑⁠י יִ֝שְׂרָאֵ֗ל בִּ⁠דְרָכַ֥⁠י יְהַלֵּֽכוּ
13.note: Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, a deep longing for Israel to obey. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Yahweh was feeling. Alternate translation: [How I long for my people to listen to me and for Israel to follow my ways]

Yahweh is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Israel would live according to my commands]

14.note: Here, **hand** represents Yahweh’s power and ability to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I would use my power]

15.note: The pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. Even though Yahweh is speaking in the first person, he refers to himself in the third person here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [would cringe before Yahweh]

Here, **time** represents the duration of their fate or condition. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and their punishment would last forever]

16.note: The pronouns **he** and **him** refer to Yahweh and Israel respectively. Even though Yahweh is speaking in the first person, he uses the third person here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I would feed Israel]

Here, **fat** represents the best and richest portion of something. Yahweh is speaking as if the finest wheat had a rich fat. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the finest wheat]
Yahweh is using this possessive form to describe the richest part of the wheat. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the richest part of the wheat]

The pronoun **you** marks an abrupt shift from the third person **him** earlier in the verse to the second person. Both refer to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I would satisfy them with honey from the rock]
